extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theology, theologians, clerics, and statesmen interested in church-state relations
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and principles for defining, electing, ordaining, and maintaining church officers (apostles, bishops, presbyters, deacons) in the early Church and under civil sovereign authority. Emphasises the relations between ecclesiastical practice and civil law/sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legality of councils' decrees
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts of Councell of the Apostles were then no Laws, but Councells; the Books of the New Testament could not be made Laws by any other authority then that of Kings, or Soveraign Assemblies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Councils' acts are conditions proposed to converts (accept or refuse at their peril) rather than binding civil laws for all Christians, unless backed by a civil sovereign with legislative power. 'Seeing then the Acts of Councell of the Apostles, were then no Laws, but Councells; much lesse are Laws the Acts of any other Doctors, or Councells since, if assembled without the Authority of the Civill Soveraign.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Councils' obligations versus personal sin
rubrics_metrics.description: Burthens which the Apostles might lay on converts are to be understood as Conditions (proposed to those that sought Salvation) which they might accept or refuse without a new sin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to adopt these conditions may hazard exclusion from salvation but does not necessarily create new civil or canonical sins enforceable as law; distinction drawn between moral/religious consequence and civil obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostleship essential mark: witness of the Resurrection
rubrics_metrics.description: The specific and essential mark, whereby the Apostleship was distinguished from other Magisteracy Ecclesiasticall, was to be Martyrs (Witnesses of our Saviours Resurrection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An Apostle must have 'companyed with us...beginning from the Baptisme of John unto that same day that he was taken up from us' or have seen the Lord after his passion (Acts 1.21-22) — the testimony of the Resurrection is the necessary property of an Apostle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of ecclesiastical offices: magisterial vs ministerial
rubrics_metrics.description: Some ecclesiastical officers were Magisteriall (preaching the Gospel, administering Sacraments and Divine Service, teaching faith and manners); some were Ministeriall (Deacons, appointed to administration of the secular necessities of the Church).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magisterial offices are concerned with spiritual teaching and sacraments (Ministers of the Word = Ministers of Christ). Ministerial offices serve the congregation's temporal needs (serving tables, revenue, house of prayer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interchangeability of early pastoral titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Bishop, Pastor, Elder, Doctor (Teacher) were but so many divers names of the same Office in the time of the Apostles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early church had no coercive government; distinctions of title did not imply distinct coercive authorities — authority was by doctrine and persuading, not compulsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gifts versus offices: evangelists and prophets
rubrics_metrics.description: By the names of Evangelists and Prophets is not signified any Office, but severall Gifts (e.g., writing the life and acts of our Saviour; interpreting the Old Testament; special revelations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession of spiritual gifts (languages, miracles, prophecy, evangelism) does not in itself constitute an Officer in the Church; only due calling and election to a teaching charge creates an office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of ordination/election: assembly plurality
rubrics_metrics.description: Presbyters and other officers were ordained by Assemblies of Christians in each city; the Apostles presided — 'When they had Ordained them Elders by the Holding up of Hands in every Congregation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original practice was election by plurality of suffrages (hands up, voices, ballots, beans/stones). Apostles acted as presidents to call assemblies, count votes, declare election, bless/confirm (consecration). Where votes were equal, the president could decide by adding his own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of Apostles and elders is congregational
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: Matthias chosen by the congregation of about 120 Christians by lot; Paul and Barnabas' mission was authorized by the particular Church of Antioch — the Church declared and authorized the calling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when called by the Holy Ghost, the declaration and authorization of apostles came from the local church; ordination was an act of the congregation, not of a single preceding bishop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for deacons and presbyters
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing deacons, the Apostles instructed: 'looke you out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost, and of Wisdome.' The multitude chose them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection criteria include good repute, fullness of the Holy Spirit, wisdom; the congregation exercises the choice after Apostolic guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecclesiastical revenue under Mosaic and civil authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Old Testament, the Tribe of Levi had no land inheritance; they were assigned tithes and offerings for maintenance — this right of tithes and offerings was constituted by the Civill Power (God as King then).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The priests' maintenance derived from public revenue under the sovereign; therefore rights like tithes are matters of civil law rather than inherent ecclesiastical prerogative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance of ministers in early Christian practice: voluntary benevolence
rubrics_metrics.description: After our Saviours Ascension, the Christians of every City lived in Common on money made of sale of lands and voluntary contributions; there was no certain maintenance fixed — ministerial support was voluntary benevolence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pastors' maintenance before state regulation depended on voluntary contributions of believers; no fixed tithes or legally enforced incomes until emperors/civil sovereigns legislated otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of pastors' allowances
rubrics_metrics.description: Though 'they which preach the Gospel should live of the Gospel,' Pastors were not to determine the quantity or kind of their own allowance; allowance must be determined by the gratitude and liberality of particular men or by the whole Congregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pastors cannot unilaterally set their stipend; absent civil laws giving force to ecclesiastical acts, maintenance is a matter of congregation's voluntary provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil sovereign as Supreme Pastor with appointment rights
rubrics_metrics.description: In every Christian Common-wealth, the Civill Soveraign is the Supreme Pastor, to whose charge the whole flock of his Subjects is committed, and consequently it is by his authority that all other Pastors are made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The right to judge what doctrines are fit for peace and to ordain pastors is inseparably annexed to sovereign power; actions done by subjects in the sovereign's dominion (e.g., electing a pastor) are acts done by the sovereign's authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastoral authority: jure divino vs jure civili
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pastorall Authority Of Soveraigns is De Jure Divino (by immediate Authority from God); the authority of other Pastors is Jure Civili (by the Authority of the Civil Soveraign).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only sovereigns may claim direct divine title (e.g., 'Dei Gratia Rex'); bishops and other ministers must acknowledge their authority as derived from the civil power (begin mandates 'By the favour of the Kings Majesty' or 'In his Majesties Name').

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign's theoretical power to perform pastoral functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian Kings, being Supreme Pastors, have the power not only to preach but also to baptize, to administer the Lord's Supper, and to consecrate temples and pastors, even if in practice they delegate these acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical non-performance is explained by the sovereign's broader duties (government, war) making delegation convenient. The sovereign's capacity to perform such functions stems from office authority, not necessarily from ceremonial imposition of hands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imposition of hands as designation ceremony, not sole source of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Imposition of Hands was an ancient public ceremony designed to make certain the person or thing intended in consecrations, blessings, ordinations; used among Jews and Heathen alike to designate individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While imposition of hands publicly designates and consecrates, the text argues its role is ceremonial and convenience-based; sovereign authority may confer rights without the ordinary ceremony when necessary. Examples given: Jacob blessing Ephraim/Manasseh, Moses ordaining Joshua, Levites' consecration.
